title: Providence
subtitle: How God governs all things. Concurrence, primary and secondary causes, and the Reformed, Arminian, and Molinist accounts of his rule.
triageNote: That God governs the world He made, that nothing happens outside His knowledge and will, that He works all things toward His ends, is held by the whole church. It sits near the center of the faith. The argument here is not whether God rules but how, how His control and our real actions fit together, how His decree relates to our freedom and to the existence of evil. That question divides Reformed from Arminian from Molinist. It has done so among people who pray to the same sovereign Lord and trust Him in the same dark. Confess the providence. Hold your account of its inner workings with humility. Here Scripture gives us the fact of God's rule far more plainly than the mechanism of it.
question:
When a sparrow falls, when a lot is cast and lands, when wicked men crucify the Lord of glory and God means it for salvation, what exactly is God doing. The Bible says He works all things according to the counsel of His will, that He numbers the hairs of your head, that not a sparrow falls apart from the Father. It also holds people fully responsible for their choices, calls them to repent, grieves over their sin, and never once excuses a sinner on the ground that God decreed it. So how does God's complete government of the world relate to the real causes inside it, the weather, the human will, the free decisions that history is made of. Does He cause everything directly, work through secondary causes, permit what He hates, or somehow know and use the free choices His creatures would make. The doctrine of providence is the church's attempt to say how the King runs His world. The great traditions answer the how differently while confessing the that together.

The word itself carries the question. Providence comes from providere, to see ahead and to provide, and the church has always meant by it more than mere foresight. It means a governing care that reaches every creature and every event, what the older divines divided into preservation (God upholding all that exists from one moment to the next), concurrence (God working in and through the actions of His creatures), and government (God directing all things toward His appointed ends). The dispute on this page is not over preservation, which all confess, but over concurrence and government, the precise place where the divine cause and the creaturely cause meet. Aquinas located God as the first cause working through real secondary causes, so that to deny the creature its causality would, he argued, detract from the power of the Creator rather than honor it. Calvin pressed the rule of God down to the smallest detail and called bare foreknowledge a frigid notion next to it. Luis de Molina, writing in 1588, proposed that God knows what every free creature would do in any circumstance and governs by means of that knowledge. Open theists in our own time have asked whether the future of free choices is even there to be known in advance. Each of these is a different answer to one question. How can it be wholly true at once that God works all things and that the sinner, not God, is the author of his sin. Scripture asserts both without strain and rarely stops to explain how. The traditions on this page are the church reasoning carefully in the space between the two assertions.
whyItMatters:
Providence is not a seminar topic. It is the doctrine you reach for at a hospital bedside, at a graveside, in the hour the diagnosis comes or the marriage ends or the child does not come home. The question is never abstract then. Did God do this. Did God allow this. Could God have stopped this, and if He could, what does it mean that He did not. Everything you believe about how God governs the world is cashed out in what you can honestly say to a person in the dark, and to yourself. The Heidelberg Catechism is famous for one answer to that question, that I am not my own but belong to my faithful Savior, and that all things are governed by His hand so that not a hair can fall without the will of my Father in heaven. People have died holding that sentence. Whether it is true, and in what sense, is what this page is about.

Get it wrong in one direction and you make God the author of evil, the one who pulls every string including the cruel ones. Then you cannot worship Him without flinching. Get it wrong in the other direction and you make God a bystander, well-meaning but finally helpless, hoping things work out. Then you cannot rest in Him, because He is not actually in charge. The historic accounts of providence are all trying to hold two things the Bible refuses to let go of at once. God genuinely rules everything. And He is in no way the doer of sin. How they hold those two is the whole argument. The argument matters because the comfort matters. And the danger runs both ways. A doctrine of meticulous control, carelessly stated at the wrong moment, can sound to a grieving mother as though God scheduled the death of her son. A doctrine of permission, carelessly stated, can leave a frightened man wondering whether God was simply unable to help. The accounts on this page are not abstractions competing for elegance. They are attempts to keep both halves of the truth available to a person who needs both at once.

It also shapes how you pray. If God has fixed everything by an eternal decree, what is prayer doing. If God responds to the free choices of His creatures, is He learning, waiting, reacting. Each account on this page gives a different texture to the life of prayer and the experience of guidance, to how you read a closed door or an answered request, to whether you say that God changed His mind or that God ordained the prayer as part of how He always meant to act. It bears as well on the oldest objection to the faith, the problem of evil, the question Boethius wrestled in a prison cell and Augustine before him, of how a world ruled by a good and almighty God can hold so much that is neither good nor explained. Your account of providence is, in the end, the shape of your answer to that. So you are not choosing a theory. You are choosing how to stand in front of your own life, and in front of the suffering of people you love, and in front of the God who has not told you everything but has told you enough to trust Him.

positions.name: The Reformed account
positions.inOneLine: God ordains and governs all that comes to pass, working through real secondary causes. Nothing is outside His sovereign decree. And yet He is never the author of sin.
positions.bestCase:
Let me begin with the verse that anchors me, because everything I say flows from it. Paul writes that God works all things according to the counsel of His will. Not some things. Not the big things while the small ones drift. All things, and according to a counsel, a settled purpose formed before the foundation of the world. I take that to mean exactly what it says. There is no maverick molecule, no rogue event, nothing that happens by an accident God did not foresee and ordain. The casting of the lot is from the Lord. The king's heart is a stream the Lord turns wherever He will. The sparrow does not fall apart from your Father. The very hairs of your head are numbered. This is not a grim doctrine to me. It is the deepest comfort I know. It means that nothing that touches my life has slipped past my Father's hand, and that the suffering I cannot understand is not loose in the world but held inside a purpose I will one day be able to bless.

Now hear the distinction that keeps this from being fatalism, because everything turns on it. God ordains the ends and He ordains the means, and the means are real. This is no Reformed novelty. Thomas Aquinas taught long before Calvin that God works through secondary causes, that He grants creatures genuine causal power, and that to deny the creature its proper action would diminish rather than magnify the Creator who gave it. Calvin took up the same conviction and pressed it through the whole of life, insisting that what looks to us like chance is in truth directed by God, and calling bare foreknowledge a cold and lifeless thing next to active rule. The Westminster Confession states it with a precision I love. God orders all things to fall out according to the nature of second causes, either necessarily, freely, or contingently. That phrase, the nature of second causes, is the whole answer to the charge that I make men puppets. When you choose, you really choose. The choice is yours, arising from your own desires, your own deliberation, with no gun to your head. And that real choice of yours is also, at a higher level, ordained by God, who works through it rather than around it. This is concurrence, the first cause and the second cause fully operative in one event on different levels. It is no contradiction, because the two are not causes of the same kind competing for the same room. It works the way an author writes a character who truly acts within the story the author truly governs. Macbeth really chooses the murder, and Shakespeare wrote every word. God does not compete with your will. He establishes it. And this is why I hold to compatibilism, the conviction that freedom is doing what you most want to do, not the power to act apart from any settled nature, so that a will moved by its own desires and ordained by God is free in the only sense that has ever mattered.

What about evil, the hard case that every account of providence must finally face. I will not flinch from it. The clearest text in the Bible on providence and evil is Joseph's word to his brothers. You meant it for evil, but God meant it for good. Notice the grammar. The same event, the selling of Joseph, has two authors with two intentions. The brothers meant evil, and they are guilty, fully, and God meant good, and He is holy, fully. God ordained the act without committing the sin. He ordained it for a righteous end while they did it from a wicked heart. The cross is the supreme case. Peter says Jesus was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and in the same breath says you crucified Him by the hands of lawless men. The believers in Acts pray it even more plainly, that Herod and Pilate did whatever God's hand and plan had predestined to take place. Ordained and guilty, both, at once. The classic distinction I lean on here is between God's positive willing of good and His willing to permit evil for ends that are themselves good, a willing permission, not a bare one, since nothing escapes His decree. I hold that the wickedness of the act belongs wholly to the creature and the ordination of it for good belongs wholly to God. I do not pretend I can fully see the seam where they meet. I confess a mystery there rather than soften either truth, and I notice that Scripture itself never resolves the seam either, but stands on both sides of it without apology.

Here is what I struggle with, and I will say it plainly. The hardest pressure on my view is the love of God for those who finally perish and the sincerity of God's grief over sin He has, on my account, ordained. Suppose God ordains all that comes to pass, including the sin and the unbelief. In what sense does He truly desire the repentance He commands, and truly grieve the death of the wicked, as Ezekiel says He does, and as Jesus does when He weeps over a city that would not be gathered. I answer with the old distinction between God's revealed will, what He commands and delights in and sincerely offers to all, and His secret will, what He decrees to bring to pass. I believe both are real and that the tension between them is the same tension we see in Jesus Himself, who genuinely wept over the Jerusalem He had not chosen to gather. But I admit the relationship between the two wills is the deep water of my position, the place I most have to trust that God is good in ways I cannot fully trace. I would rather hold a sovereign God I cannot fully explain than a manageable God who is not finally in charge of the world I have to live and die in.
advocates: D. A. Carson (How Long, O Lord?)

positions.name: The Arminian account
positions.inOneLine: God governs all things and permits much that He does not cause, granting creatures genuine freedom. So sin and evil arise from the will of the creature, never from the will of God.
positions.bestCase:
Let me say first what I am not, because I am almost always met as a denial before I am met as a claim. I am not saying God is weak, or surprised, or scrambling to keep up with a world that got away from Him. I confess that God is sovereign over all things, that He knows the end from the beginning, that He upholds the universe and works toward His purposes with a power nothing can defeat, that His foreknowledge is exhaustive and certain. Arminius himself, the man whose name I carry, affirmed the full foreknowledge of God and the providence that governs all, and Wesley after him preached the rule of God over every detail of a believer's life as warmly as any Calvinist ever has. My quarrel is not with God's sovereignty. It is with one particular account of how that sovereignty operates, the account that makes God the one who ordains the very sins He then condemns. I cannot reconcile that with the character of the God revealed in Jesus Christ. And I think Scripture itself stops me.

Here is the heart of it. The Bible is full of God grieving. God is grieved to His heart that He made man. God says, what more was there to do for my vineyard that I have not done. Through Ezekiel He asks whether He has any pleasure in the death of the wicked, and answers His own question, no, but rather that he should turn and live. Christ weeps over Jerusalem, how often I would have gathered your children, and you were not willing. If God ordains every event, including every refusal of His grace, then these tears are a kind of theater, God grieving over what He Himself decreed and could at any moment have decreed otherwise. I do not believe the God of the gospel weeps at a play He wrote. I believe the grief is real because the resistance is real, because God genuinely offers Himself and creatures genuinely, terribly, can say no. The you were not willing is the most important phrase in my theology of providence. It means the human will is a real cause, not a channel for the divine will wearing a mask. And this is why I hold to libertarian freedom, the conviction that when a creature faces a genuine choice he could truly have done otherwise, for without that the command to repent, the offer of grace, and the guilt of refusing it all lose their meaning.

So how do I hold God's universal government together with real creaturely freedom. Through the category of permission, which is not a dodge but a serious theological tool the church has used since Augustine and before. God governs by two modes, what He actively does and what He permits. He actively works all good, for every good and perfect gift comes down from the Father of lights, in whom there is no shadow of turning. And He permits, allows within His sovereign sufferance, the evil that creatures choose. It is evil He could prevent but for wise reasons does not, evil He hates and will judge and is even now turning toward ends it never intended. James warns us pointedly never to say that God tempts us to evil, for He tempts no one, and locates the source of sin instead in each person being lured by his own desire. This is the strength of providence rightly understood. God is so completely in command that He can give His creatures real freedom, including the freedom to wound Him, and still bend every wound toward the good He purposed. He did not have to ordain Joseph's brothers sin to bring good out of it. He permitted their freely chosen evil and overruled it, so that what they meant for evil He meant for good. That is a greater sovereignty, not a lesser one, because it governs even what it did not author, and it leaves the sin wholly theirs and the redemption wholly His.

Let me name the texts that I find hardest, because honesty requires it. The cross is the great difficulty for me. Peter says Jesus was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and the prayer in Acts speaks of what God's hand had predestined to take place, and that language is stronger than mere permission. It sounds like a plan that included the very act. I answer that God foreknew and purposed the giving of His Son from before the foundation of the world, and worked through the freely chosen wickedness of men without authoring that wickedness, so that the predestined thing is the redemption accomplished, not the malice of Judas. The phrase delivered up describes the Father's deliberate offering of the Son more than His scripting of any traitor. But I grant this is the place my distinction between active will and permission is stretched thinnest, where my critics press me hardest, and they are not wrong to press. And I feel the weight of all things in Ephesians 1:11. I read it as God working out His overarching redemptive purpose in Christ through all things rather than as God decreeing each thing severally, and I note that the chapter is about His purpose for the church, not a treatise on the cause of every event. But I know the Reformed reader hears the verse the other way, and I do not pretend the word all makes my reading effortless. I hold permission because I cannot make the God of Gethsemane the secret author of Judas, nor the weeping Christ the playwright of the refusal He wept over. I will pay the exegetical cost of that conviction before I will pay the theological one.
advocates: the classic Arminian and Wesleyan tradition

positions.name: The Molinist account
positions.inOneLine: God knows what every free creature would do in every possible situation. Through that knowledge He sovereignly arranges the world to accomplish His purposes, while leaving creaturely freedom fully intact.
positions.bestCase:
I want to offer you what I believe is the most carefully built bridge across the very gap the other two accounts strain over. It is the gap between God ordaining everything and creatures being genuinely free. The bridge has a name from its sixteenth-century architect, the Spanish Jesuit Luis de Molina, who set it out in his great work the Concordia of 1588, whose very title announces the aim, the harmony of free choice with the gifts of grace, foreknowledge, providence, and predestination. It rests on a single, powerful idea. God knows not only everything that will happen and everything that could happen, but everything that would happen, the free choices each creature would make in any circumstance God might place him in. Theologians call this middle knowledge, scientia media, because it sits between two other kinds of divine knowledge, His natural knowledge of all that is possible and necessary, and His free knowledge of all that He has decided to do. The middle knowledge comes logically before God decrees anything, and that order is the whole secret of the account.

Let me show you why this changes everything. Picture God before creation, contemplating not just possible worlds but, within them, what every possible free person would freely do in every possible setting. He knows that if He places this person in these exact circumstances, she will freely choose this, and if in those circumstances, she will freely choose that. None of it is forced. In each case she does exactly what she wants, and could have done otherwise. But because God knows all of it, He can choose which world to actualize. He selects from the immense range of feasible worlds, the worlds it is genuinely open to Him to bring about given how free creatures would in fact behave, the one in which free creatures, doing freely what they would do, accomplish His sovereign purposes. So God's providence is total and meticulous down to the last detail, for He has sovereignly arranged the whole. And human freedom is libertarian and real, because in every actual choice the person could have done otherwise. The Reformed believer gets the meticulous sovereignty he treasures, with nothing left to chance. The Arminian gets the genuine freedom and the real human no she will not surrender. And neither has to bend. This is why William Lane Craig calls middle knowledge perhaps the single most fruitful idea ever conceived for the doctrine of providence.

Now watch it handle the hardest case, the cross. Scripture says, impossibly for the other views to hold together easily, that Jesus was delivered by the definite plan and foreknowledge of God and crucified by the hands of lawless men, and that Herod and Pilate did whatever God's hand and plan had predestined to take place. Middle knowledge holds both with no strain. God knew what Herod, Pilate, the chief priests, and Judas would freely do if placed in the circumstances of first-century Jerusalem with the Son of God in their midst. Knowing it, He sovereignly brought about exactly those circumstances, and they freely did what He foreknew they would do. So the cross was both definitely planned and freely committed wickedness. God did not implant the betrayal in Judas heart. He placed Judas, knowing the heart Judas would bring. The plan is God's and the sin is Judas, cleanly, on two different grounds. And I would point you to the texts that seem to me to show this faculty at work in plain narrative. David asks at Keilah whether Saul will come down and whether the men of the city will surrender him, and God answers that they would, so David flees and neither thing ever comes to pass, which means God knew truly what free men would have done in a situation that never happened. Jesus says that if the mighty works done in Chorazin had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented in sackcloth and ashes. That is the counterfactual knowledge of free choices, stated by the Lord Himself. I find no other model that lets me read Acts 2:23 without softening either half.

Where am I pressed hardest, and I will not hide it. The deepest objection to my view is called the grounding objection, and it is serious, pressed by Reformed and open theist critics alike. What makes the counterfactuals of creaturely freedom true before God creates anyone. If Peter does not yet exist, what is it that grounds the fact that this Peter, in these circumstances, would freely deny Christ three times. The choice is supposed to be free, so it cannot be grounded in God's decree, or I lose the very freedom I built the whole system to protect. The Reformed critic says the only thing that could make such a truth certain is God's own decree, which collapses my view back into theirs. The open theist says that absent such grounding there simply is no fact there yet to be known, since the choice has not been made. I answer that these are truths about what free persons would do, true in themselves, known by an omniscient God precisely because He knows every truth there is. I do not think their lacking a prior cause makes them less real, since free choices by their very nature are not produced by something prior to the chooser, and it would be strange to demand a prior cause for the very thing I am calling uncaused and free. But I grant this is the philosophical knife-edge my whole account balances on, and a thoughtful Reformed or Arminian or open theist critic will go straight for it, and should. I hold middle knowledge because it is the one model I have found that lets me affirm, without fudging, both the all of Ephesians and the you were not willing of Matthew. I would rather defend a hard philosophical point than surrender either verse.
advocates: William Lane Craig (The Only Wise God)
Alvin Plantinga (on free will, broadly Molinist)
Thomas Flint (Divine Providence: The Molinist Account)

biblicalEvidence.summary: In Him we have obtained an inheritance, having been predestined according to the purpose of Him who works all things according to the counsel of His will. The phrase all things according to the counsel of His will is the Reformed charter for meticulous providence. God works out everything according to a settled purpose.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hardest for the Arminian account. It must read all things as God's overarching purpose worked through events rather than His decree of each event.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The Arminian reads works all things as God accomplishing His grand redemptive purpose through all that happens, governing the whole without scripting each part. It notes the context is God's purpose in Christ for the church, not a treatise on every event. The Molinist reads it as God sovereignly actualizing, through His middle knowledge, the one world in which all things together fulfill His counsel, which preserves both the all and creaturely freedom.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Shared, claimed most strongly by the Reformed account
biblicalEvidence.summary: As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive. One event, the selling of Joseph, carries two intentions, the brothers' evil and God's good, the brothers guilty and God holy.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: It presses every view. It holds together a freely chosen human evil and a divine intention in the same act, which no account finds simple.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The Reformed reads God meant it as God's positive ordination of the event for good, the brothers' evil and God's purpose concurring in one act. The Arminian reads it as God overruling and redeeming a freely chosen evil He permitted but did not author, the greater sovereignty that governs even what it did not cause. The Molinist reads it as God arranging circumstances knowing what the brothers would freely choose, so the good was planned through their foreknown free act.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Shared, the test case for all three
biblicalEvidence.summary: Jesus was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and you crucified Him by the hands of lawless men. Later, Herod and Pilate gathered to do whatever God's hand and plan had predestined to take place. The cross is both definitely planned by God and freely committed wickedness by men.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hardest for the Arminian account, since the language goes beyond bare permission to a definite plan that predestined what would take place. It is also a standing challenge to any view that cannot hold plan and guilt together.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The Reformed reads it as the clearest proof of meticulous providence, ordained and guilty at once. The Arminian reads delivered up as the Father's deliberate giving of the Son and predestined as God's settled purpose to save through the cross, worked out through freely chosen sin He did not author. The Molinist reads it as God placing the actors in circumstances where He knew, by middle knowledge, exactly what they would freely do, so the plan is God's and the sin is theirs without remainder.

biblicalEvidence.summary: The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the Lord. The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the Lord, and He turns it wherever He will. Even the random fall of a lot and the will of a powerful king are governed by God down to the detail.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Pressed against accounts that stress creaturely autonomy. God is said to direct even the lot and the king's heart.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The Arminian reads these as God's freedom to direct outcomes and incline hearts when His purposes require it, not a claim that He determines every human choice always. It notes proverbs state general truths about God's rule. The Molinist reads them as God achieving the outcome He wills through His knowledge of how the lot would fall and how the king would freely respond, sovereignty exercised through, not against, the secondary causes.

biblicalEvidence.summary: How often would I have gathered your children, and you were not willing. Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked, declares the Lord, and not rather that he should turn and live. God's expressed desire for repentance, and human resistance to it, are stated as real.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hardest for the Reformed account. It must explain how God genuinely desires what He has, on its view, not decreed, by distinguishing God's revealed will from His secret will.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The Reformed reads these as God's revealed will, His genuine command and delight in repentance, which is real and distinct from His secret decree. So the grief is not theater but the expression of God's true moral character. The Molinist reads them as God's genuine desire for the salvation of all, satisfied within the constraints of a world of free creatures, some of whom God foreknew would refuse Him in any feasible world.

biblicalEvidence.summary: David asks whether Saul will come down and whether the men of Keilah will surrender him. God answers that they would, so David flees and the events never occur. Jesus says that if the miracles done in Chorazin had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented. God knows what free agents would do in circumstances that never come to pass.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Pressed against views with no place for counterfactuals of freedom. God here knows truly what people would freely have done in situations that did not happen.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The Reformed reads these as God's knowledge of what would follow from His own ordained arrangements, or as vivid expressions of human responsibility, not as a distinct middle knowledge prior to His decree. The Arminian reads them as God's exhaustive foreknowledge, including conditional knowledge, without committing to the full Molinist machinery of pre-volitional world-selection. The Molinist reads them as direct biblical evidence that God possesses middle knowledge of free counterfactuals, the very faculty the account is built on.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: The Arminian account, a caution to all
biblicalEvidence.summary: Let no one say when he is tempted, I am being tempted by God, for God cannot be tempted with evil, and He Himself tempts no one. Every good and perfect gift is from above. God is the source of all good and in no way the source of anyone's enticement to sin.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: A standing caution to any account that drifts toward making God the cause of sin. The Reformed must show its concurrence does not make God the author of evil.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The Reformed reads this as confirming its own careful line. God ordains that sin occur for righteous ends but is never its tempter or author. The evil belongs wholly to the creature's desire, which the next verses locate in each person being lured by his own desire. The Molinist reads it as God arranging circumstances but never implanting the sinful desire, which the creature freely brings. All three agree the verse forbids ever tracing the sinfulness of sin back to God.

weighing:
My judgment, offered as one pastor reasoning aloud and not as a ruling you must accept. I hold this one with particular care, because providence is the doctrine people are clutching when they are least able to bear a careless word.

I find myself standing closest to the Reformed account, and I will tell you honestly why. It is the reading that lets the word all in Ephesians 1:11 mean all. And it lets Acts 2:23 say what it says without my having to file down either edge, the definite plan or the lawless hands. When I am at a bedside, I want to be able to say that nothing here has escaped my Father's hand. Only an account in which God truly governs everything lets me say that and mean it. The Reformed distinction between primary and secondary causes, God working through my real choices rather than around them, is to me the most satisfying thing the tradition has produced. It refuses to make me a puppet while refusing to make God a spectator.

But I will not pretend the other rooms have nothing I need. The Arminian presses me exactly where I am weakest, on the tears of God, on the you were not willing of Jesus over Jerusalem. I take that pressure seriously, because a doctrine of providence that cannot account for the genuine grief of God has lost something essential about His character. I lean on the old distinction between God's revealed and secret will to answer it. I believe the distinction is real, but I hold it as a place of trust more than a place of full sight. And the Molinist has given me the most ingenious tool anyone has built for this problem, middle knowledge. On my better days I think it may be exactly right, a way to say sovereignty and freedom together without fudging either. On my harder days the grounding objection troubles me, the question of what makes those free counterfactuals true before anyone exists, and I cannot make it fully go away.

So I land here, loosely. I trust a God who truly governs all things and is in no way the author of any sin. And I confess that the seam where those two truths meet runs down into a darkness I cannot see the bottom of. I would rather worship a sovereign God whose ways I cannot fully trace than tidy Him into a theory I can hold in one hand. Where exactly the mechanism lies, decree, permission, or middle knowledge, I hold with an open hand. I have learned more about providence from believers who land differently than I have from those who simply agree with me.
charitableDisagreement:
It is easy to turn this into a contest over who loves God's sovereignty most, with the Reformed claiming the high ground of God's glory and dismissing everyone else as man-centered. Or into a contest over who loves God's goodness most, with the Arminian claiming the high ground of God's love and dismissing the Reformed as worshiping a tyrant. Both contests are uncharitable. Both miss what is actually happening, which is three serious attempts to hold the same two biblical truths at once.

Hear what each is guarding. The Reformed is guarding the comfort that nothing, nothing at all, falls outside the Father's hand, and the refusal to let any corner of the world become a place where God is not King. The Arminian is guarding the goodness of God against ever becoming the secret author of the evil He weeps over, and the reality of the human no that makes the human yes mean something. The Molinist is guarding the conviction that you do not have to choose between those two. A wise enough God can have both His meticulous rule and our real freedom, and the gospel need not be built on surrendering either. These are not three levels of faithfulness. They are three guards posted around the same treasure, each watching the wall the others have their backs to.

So is this a hill to die on. The fact of providence, that God really governs the world and works all things toward His good ends, is near the center of the faith. A believer who has lost it has lost the ground he stands on when the night comes. But the mechanism of providence, the in-house argument among Reformed and Arminian and Molinist over how decree and freedom and permission fit together, is a second-order question. Faithful churches have carried it side by side for centuries, in the same pews, at the same Table. Hold the providence with your whole weight. Hold your theory of its inner workings with a lighter hand. Be slow to question the faith of the brother who trusts the same sovereign Lord through a different account of how He rules. At the graveside, all three of these believers are saying the same thing. He has not let go of us, and He never will.

relatedDebates.note: Providence and the freedom debate are the same coin seen from two sides. How God governs all things depends on what human freedom is, compatibilist or libertarian. The next page in this set takes up the nature of freedom directly, where Molinism and compatibilism and libertarian freedom are argued on their own terms.

Every account of providence is finally tested at the problem of evil. If God governs all things and is wholly good, why is there so much suffering and sin. The distinctions made here, primary and secondary causes, permission, middle knowledge, are largely tools forged to answer that question without making God its author.

relatedDebates.topic: Election and the freedom of grace
relatedDebates.note: The doctrine of salvation, taken up on the soteriology page, applies these very accounts of providence to the question of how a person comes to faith. It asks whether grace is irresistible, whether the will cooperates, whether God elects on the basis of foreseen faith. Where you land on providence quietly decides much of where you land there.

If God has ordained all that comes to pass, what does prayer accomplish, and how can the unchanging God be moved by it. Each account of providence gives a different texture to petition. The relationship between God's settled purpose and the prayers He ordains as part of how that purpose comes about is its own rich and practical discussion.
